title: Work & Kinetic Energy
summary: Work is force acting through a distance, $W=Fd\cos\theta$ (or $\int F\,dx$ for varying force). The work–energy theorem says net work equals the change in kinetic energy, $W_{net}=\Delta KE$. Power is the rate of doing work.

work.plain: Energy transferred by a force over a distance.

work-energy theorem.plain: Net work equals change in kinetic energy.

variable force work.plain: Work when force changes with position.

dot product.in_class: Picks out the component of force along motion.

concept_sections.heading: Work by a constant force
concept_sections.explanation: Work is $W=Fd\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between force and displacement. A perpendicular force does no work; an opposing force does negative work.

concept_sections.heading: Work by a variable force
concept_sections.explanation: When force depends on position, work is the integral $W=\int F\,dx$ — the area under the force–position graph. A spring gives $W=\tfrac12kx^2$.

concept_sections.heading: Kinetic energy
concept_sections.explanation: A moving mass carries $KE=\tfrac12mv^2$. It scales with the square of speed — doubling speed quadruples the energy.

concept_sections.heading: The work–energy theorem
concept_sections.explanation: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: $W_{net}=\tfrac12mv_f^2-\tfrac12mv_i^2$. This links forces to speed changes without needing acceleration explicitly.
math_steps: Solve for the unknown speed or distance.

concept_sections.heading: Power
concept_sections.explanation: Power is how fast work is done: $P=W/t$, or $P=Fv$ for a force acting at speed $v$. Measured in watts.
math_steps: Divide work by time, or use $P=Fv$.

real_world_examples.title: Lifting weights
real_world_examples.scenario: Raising a barbell a set height.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Work $W=mgh$ is done against gravity; power depends on how fast you lift.

real_world_examples.title: A car engine's power
real_world_examples.scenario: An engine sustains speed against drag.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: $P=Fv$ gives the power needed to overcome resistance at a given speed.

real_world_examples.title: A compressed spring launcher
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The stored $\tfrac12kx^2$ becomes the ball's kinetic energy.
